summary: AE + SE met with VertexHealth ML and platform team to align POC success criteria: 99th percentile tail latency < 250ms for short prompts and 95% availability across 8-hour window; target throughput 200 reqs/s steady, 800 rps burst. Discussed benchmark harness integration, customer scripts, and whether to exercise streaming vs non-streaming APIs for the workload. Agreed next steps: share harness adapter, customer to provide scripts, schedule initial benchmark run next week, and Redwood to send SOW.
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-08-18 16:00 PDT | Duration ~52 minutes | Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Liam (Redwood SE), Priya (Redwood SE), Daniel (VertexHealth ML), Sofia (VertexHealth Platform), Aisha (VertexHealth Security), Tom (VertexHealth Product)

[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick roll call?
[00:05] Daniel Park: daniel here, hi.
[00:07] Sofia Martinez: sofia present.
[00:09] Aisha Khan: aisha on security.
[00:11] Tom Reynolds: tom here.
[00:13] Liam O'Connor: liam from redwood, thanks, we're excited to dig in.

[00:30] Maya Chen: high level goal of this call is to scope the poc — we heard the ask is SLA-driven benchmarking to validate the inference path and the streaming decision, correct?
[00:36] Daniel Park: yes, we need to verify that our patient-facing assistant can meet tail latency SLOs and scale cost-effectively. we're evaluating hosted first but may move to dedicated or private if needed.

[01:05] Priya Rao: quick clarifying q — when you say patient-facing assistant, is this mostly short-turn prompts (single-shot clinical q&a) or longer multi-turn conversations?
[01:12] Daniel Park: primarily short prompts, 16-256 tokens typically. about 80% under 64 tokens. but there's a smaller percentage (10-15%) of longer summarization flows ~300-800 tokens.

[01:40] Sofia Martinez: also platform note: we expect steady traffic of approx 200 rps during business hours, with bursts up to 800 rps on some days. latency SLO is strict: 99th percentile under 250ms for short prompts.

[02:05] Liam O'Connor: ok that helps a lot. streaming vs non-streaming becomes interesting — streaming can reduce time-to-first-token for long outputs, but adds complexity for the harness and for your client integration. for short prompts, non-streaming RPCs are often simpler and meet SLOs.

[02:45] Aisha Khan: security constraints — everything must be encrypted at rest and in transit, keys managed by our KMS. any private deployment needs to fit into our VPC and support SAML SSO + audit logs for every inference request.

[03:20] Maya Chen: understood. redwood private and dedicated support KMS integrations and audit logs; we'll include compliance doc in the pack.

[03:50] Tom Reynolds: i'd like to understand the benchmark harness expectations — what does redwood need from us to run a representative benchmark?

[04:05] Liam O'Connor: good q. at minimum we need: your customer scripts (the exact call patterns), a token distribution csv, sample payloads (including any system prompts / tool-calling samples), and an SLA matrix (which metrics matter). we'll provide a harness adapter that maps your scripts into the benchmark runner. ideally a small dockerized shim from your side that emits the same client-side behavior.

[04:45] Daniel Park: can the adapter support client-side retry/backoff behaviour and custom headers (we send session tokens)?
[04:52] Priya Rao: yes — the adapter proto supports custom headers and pluggable retry policies. small caveat: when streaming is enabled the retry semantics shift, we document the recommended pattern.

[05:20] [05:30] Sofia Martinez: latency measurement question — do you measure server-side end-to-end or client-side time-to-first-byte as well? we care about user-perceived latency.
[05:38] Liam O'Connor: we capture both: server-side token-emission latency and client-side RTT. our harness will emit per-request traces and token timelines so you can compute TTFB, TTR (time-to-response), and p99 p999.

[06:10] Maya Chen: ok let's talk acceptance criteria. what would you consider a pass for the POC?

[06:18] Daniel Park: pass if: 1) p99 tail for short prompts < 250ms for 95% of the 8-hour test window, 2) sustained throughput at 200 rps with CPU/GPU utilization under thresholds for cost predictability, 3) no PII leakage in logs and audit trail present, 4) a cost-per-1k-token estimate within our budget (we'll share budget bands).

[06:55] Priya Rao: to add, we recommend observing cold-start tails; we'll include a cold-start exercise in the benchmark. also we'll run mixed-mode traffic (80% short, 15% medium, 5% long).

[07:20] Aisha Khan: on PII: does redwood redact or is that on our side? we need assurances on in-flight and persisted data handling.

[07:28] Liam O'Connor: we don't modify customer payloads by default; data retention and redaction are configurable — for hosted we have retention controls and a delete API; for dedicated/private you control retention and can integrate KMS/HSM. we'll provide security docs and SOC2 scope details.

[08:05] Tom Reynolds: timeline — we aim to finish the POC and acceptance in 4 weeks. is that realistic?

[08:12] Maya Chen: yes, typical pilot timeline is 3-6 weeks. slotted activities: week 1 adapter + scripts handoff, week 2 initial bench run and tuning, week 3 run formal acceptance windows, week 4 wrap and exec review.

[08:45] Daniel Park: good. for the bench runs, can you simulate our burst patterns? e.g., ramp to 800 rps with a 30-min sustained burst and observe queueing behavior.

[08:53] Priya Rao: yes we can. we also can add synthetic KV cache hits/misses to mimic session-level caching. is your app using short-lived conversations or do you reuse KV cache across calls?

[09:15] Daniel Park: we reuse a per-session KV cache for multi-turn, but for the short prompts it's stateless. expect mostly cache-miss for short prompts.

[09:36] Liam O'Connor: that'll affect cost and latency — cache-hit ratio drastically reduces tokens per call for multi-turn. we'll configure the harness to include a cache-hit param but default to miss for your primary short-prompt path.

[10:00] Sofia Martinez: we need to decide streaming vs non-streaming — does the harness support both?

[10:07] Priya Rao: yes. operationally, streaming reduces time-to-first-token for long responses and smooths out some latency tails, but it imposes more state on the client side and complicates retries. for short prompts (<64 tokens) gains are marginal.

[10:40] Aisha Khan: from compliance POV streaming opens up a longer-lived connection — any additional logging surface or risk?

[10:47] Liam O'Connor: surface area grows a bit — we log connection establishment and events but you can control retention. nothing fundamentally new re: encryption. we'll note this in the security doc.

[11:10] Maya Chen: let's sketch the concrete bench plan: 1) customer provides 48 hours of representative scripts and token histogram, 2) redwood creates adapter and does one dry run, 3) we do 2 formal 2-hour acceptance windows (business hours sim) with specified mix and bursts, 4) collect logs/metrics and cost estimate, 5) review and decision. sound right?

[11:35] Daniel Park: yes. when you say cost estimate, is that cost per-1k-token or per-concurrent? we need both.

[11:42] Liam O'Connor: we'll give per-1000-token and per-hour throughput burn numbers for the model profiles used, and an expected price for hosted vs dedicated baseline.

[12:05] Tom Reynolds: about models — do you recommend quantized variants? we want to measure quality regressions during the metric runs.

[12:12] Priya Rao: we'll run two model profiles: fp16 baseline and int8 quantized variant. both will be included in the harness so you can compare latency/cost/quality. we'll attach a small eval prompt set to detect quality regressions.

[12:50] Sofia Martinez: what's the rollback/fallback plan if quality drops too much on quantized?

[12:55] Liam O'Connor: in benchmark config we have automatic fallback policies — the runtime can route to a higher-precision variant on quality triggers or p99 breach. for the POC we'll demo the fallback but real traffic routing you'd configure in production.

[13:25] Daniel Park: any special infra we need on our side for the harness? we prefer not to open broad inbound rules.

[13:31] Liam O'Connor: the harness runs from within our infra for hosted tests, but for private/dedicated we can run the harness in your VPC or you can run the driver — in the latter case we'll provide the container and a checklist. minimal outbound to Redwood endpoints required for coordination.

[14:00] Maya Chen: let's talk observability — what dashboards and artifacts you'll receive?

[14:06] Priya Rao: you'll get per-route latency histograms, token-level timelines, request/response traces, error logs, and the raw harness csv. we also share a short ops runbook for tuning batching and kv cache configs.

[14:30] Aisha Khan: can we get an artifact proving audit logs are immutable? we need to show auditors.

[14:36] Liam O'Connor: audit logs are append-only and signed in our hosted offering; for private you'll control storage but we can provide signing options. we'll include a section in the security pack.

[15:05] Tom Reynolds: about the harness adapter — what's the expected repo layout and language? we predominantly use go and kotlin on our side.

[15:12] Priya Rao: our adapter is a small go/python shim. we can provide a go starter repo that wires into your grpc or rest client. it's under a permissive license and well-documented.

[15:40] Daniel Park: latency measurements — you mentioned p999 earlier. do you recommend including p999 for final acceptance?

[15:46] Liam O'Connor: we suggest p99 and p999 observationally; for acceptance p99 is typical. p999 is useful for understanding extreme tails and may influence whether you require dedicated capacity.

[16:10] Maya Chen: any blockers we should flag now?

[16:16] Aisha Khan: we need to confirm data residency — some data must remain in region. if hosted endpoints route outside our region that could be a blocker.

[16:23] Liam O'Connor: noted — we'll map regions and provide regionally-hosted endpoints. dedicated/private avoids cross-region egress.

[16:45] Sofia Martinez: when can we have the initial adapter?

[16:49] Liam O'Connor: we'll push a prototype adapter by 2026-08-20; final adapter after we review your scripts.

[17:05] Maya Chen: ok let's do a quick recap and next steps.

[17:10] Maya Chen: recap — VertexHealth provides 48hr scripts + token hist; Redwood provides adapter + security pack; run 2x 2-hour formal windows next week; collect artifacts and produce cost & SLA report; follow-up meeting to review results.

[17:28] Daniel Park: sounds good. target to have first bench run by 2026-08-24?
[17:32] Maya Chen: yes we'll aim for 24th; liam to confirm exact 2-hour window.

[17:40] Tom Reynolds: one small ask — can you include a plain-English explainer for streaming vs non-streaming tradeoffs for our PMs?

[17:46] Priya Rao: yep we'll include a 1-page comparison in the kit.

[18:00] Maya Chen: thanks everyone. we'll follow up with the SOW and links. end call.

Notes: small transcription artifacts present — names occasionally mis-tagged (e.g., "liam" sometimes as "Liam O Connor"), filler tokens present. Shared links referenced during call: SOW template (https://redwood.example.com/sow-template), harness adapter proto repo (https://github.com/redwood/harness-adapters/vertexhealth-proto), security pack (https://redwood.example.com/security/vertexhealth-pack).
